###Part A — Examples of Conditional Statements

conditional statement lets R choose what to do based on whether a condition is TRUE or FALSE. Run each example, then change the values to see the output change.

Example A: if ... else. Choose between two outcomes for a single value.

```{r}
score <- 78

if (score >= 75) {
  print("Passed")
} else {
  print("Failed")
}
```
Example B: if ... else if ... else. Use it when there are more than two outcomes. R checks from top to bottom and stops at the first condition that is TRUE.

```{r}
score <- 86

if (score >= 90) {
  print("Excellent")
} else if (score >= 80) {
  print("Good")
} else if (score >= 75) {
  print("Fair")
} else {
  print("Needs Improvement")
}
```

Example C: ifelse() for a whole vector. if works on one value at a time. ifelse() checks every element of a vector at once, which is what you need for a column of data.

```{r}
scores <- c(92, 68, 75, 81, 59)
ifelse(scores >= 75, "Passed", "Failed")
```

Example D: combining conditions. Use & when both conditions must be true and | when at least one must be true.

```{r}
grade <- 91
attendance <- 95

if (grade >= 90 & attendance >= 90) {
  print("Honors candidate")
}
```

Question #4

Predict the output of the code below before you run it. Then run it and explain, in a comment, why you got that result.

```{r}
x <- 10
if (x > 5) {
  print("A")
} else if (x > 8) {
  print("B")
} else {
  print("C")
}
```
Why we get "A":
In an if ... else if ... else chain, R checks conditions top-to-bottom and
runs the code block for the FIRST condition that evaluates to TRUE, then skips
the remaining branches. Because x is 10, `x > 5` is already TRUE, so R
prints "A" and never reaches `else if (x > 8)` (even though 10 > 8 is also true).

Question #5

What is the difference between if and ifelse()? When would you choose each one?

if: Used for a single condition (TRUE/FALSE) and branching code flow or multi-line blocks.
ifelse(): Used for vectors to return an element-by-element result matching the vector's length.
When to choose: Use if for single checks/control flow; use ifelse() for applying a rule across every item in a vector.

###Part C: Importing the CSV File

Scenario. You are the data assistant of Mabini National High School. The registrar gave you students_grades.csv, which holds quiz, midterm, and final exam scores and attendance for 15 students. Your job is to compute each student’s final grade, decide who passed, assign grade remarks, flag students at risk, identify honors candidates, and send the cleaned results back to the registrar as CSV files.

Question #6

Import the file safely.**

```{r}
file_path <- "students_grades.csv"

if (file.exists(file_path)) {
  grades <- read.csv(file_path, stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
  print("students_grades.csv imported successfully.")
} else {
  stop(paste("File not found:", file_path))
}
```

Use if ... else to check that the file exists before importing it.

```{r}
file_path <- "students_grades.csv"

if (file.exists(file_path)) {
  grades <- read.csv(file_path, stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
  print("File imported successfully.")
} else {

}
```

Applying Conditional Statements
The registrar uses these rules. Each task adds a new column to grades.

f.1 Compute the final grade.** Any arithmetic with NA gives NA, so the student with the missing midterm will have NA as a final grade. This is expected.

```{r}
grades$FinalGrade <- 0.30 * grades$Quiz + 0.30 * grades$Midterm + 0.40 * grades$Final

head(grades[, c("StudentID", "Name", "Quiz", "Midterm", "Final", "FinalGrade")])
```

f.2 Pass or fail.** Check for NA first, because NA >= 75 gives NA, not TRUE or FALSE.
```{r}
grades$Result <- ifelse(
  is.na(grades$FinalGrade),
  "Incomplete",
  ifelse(grades$FinalGrade >= 75, "Passed", "Failed")
)

table(grades$Result, useNA = "ifany")
```

f.3 Grade remarks.** Replace each ___ with the correct cutoff or label, then change eval=FALSE to eval=TRUE in the chunk header.

```{r}
grades$Remarks <- ifelse(
  is.na(grades$FinalGrade),
  "Incomplete",
  ifelse(
    grades$FinalGrade >= 90,
    "Excellent",
    ifelse(
      grades$FinalGrade >= 85,
      "Very Good",
      ifelse(
        grades$FinalGrade >= 80,
        "Good",
        ifelse(
          grades$FinalGrade >= 75,
          "Fair",
          "Needs Improvement"
        )
      )
    )
  )
)

table(grades$Remarks, useNA = "ifany")
```

f.4 Attendance flag.** Write one ifelse() statement that creates a column AttendanceFlag with "At Risk" when Attendance is below 80 and "OK" otherwise.
```{r}
grades$AttendanceFlag <- ifelse(
  is.na(grades$Attendance),
  NA,
  ifelse(grades$Attendance < 80, "At Risk", "OK")
)

table(grades$AttendanceFlag, useNA = "ifany")
```

f.5 Honors candidates.** Write one ifelse() statement that creates a column Honors with "Yes" or "No". Use & to require both a final grade of 90 or higher and attendance of 90 or higher. Students with a missing final grade must get "No". Hint: use !is.na(grades$FinalGrade) as the first condition.

```{r}
grades$Honors <- ifelse(
  !is.na(grades$FinalGrade) & !is.na(grades$Attendance) &
    grades$FinalGrade >= 90 & grades$Attendance >= 90,
  "Yes",
  "No"
)

table(grades$Honors, useNA = "ifany")
```

f.6 if ... else if inside a loop.** ifelse() works on a whole column, but a plain if handles one value at a time. To use if on a column you must loop over the rows.
```{r}
loop_result <- character(nrow(grades))

for (i in seq_len(nrow(grades))) {
  fg <- grades$FinalGrade[i]
  if (is.na(fg)) {
    loop_result[i] <- "Incomplete"
  } else if (fg >= 75) {
    loop_result[i] <- "Passed"
  } else {
    loop_result[i] <- "Failed"
  }
}

grades$LoopResult <- loop_result
table(grades$LoopResult, useNA = "ifany")
```

f.7 Now try if (grades$FinalGrade >= 75) print("Passed") on its own in the Console. Explain the error or warning R gives and why the loop version avoids it.
```{r}
# Running `if (grades$FinalGrade >= 75) print("Passed")` on its own fails or warns
# because `grades$FinalGrade >= 75` returns a logical vector of multiple values
# (and possibly NA), whereas `if ()` expects a single scalar TRUE or FALSE.
# The `for` loop avoids this by passing one scalar element `grades$FinalGrade[i]`
# per iteration and checking `is.na(fg)` before numeric comparisons.
```
Error in if (grades$FinalGrade >= 75) print("Passed") :
  the condition has length > 1
  
  f.8 — Summarize Results
```{r}
passed_n <- sum(grades$Result == "Passed", na.rm = TRUE)
at_risk_n <- sum(grades$AttendanceFlag == "At Risk", na.rm = TRUE)
honors_n <- sum(grades$Honors == "Yes", na.rm = TRUE)

cat("Passed:", passed_n, "\n")
cat("At Risk:", at_risk_n, "\n")
cat("Honors candidates:", honors_n, "\n")


```
  
f.9 Check grades should now have 12 columns (7 original plus FinalGrade, Result, Remarks, AttendanceFlag, Honors).

```{r}
# Remove temporary loop column if kept, leaving the 7 original + 5 new columns
grades$LoopResult <- NULL

ncol(grades)
names(grades)
```

###Part D: Exporting Results to .csv

Question #7

Export the full processed table.** The argument row.names = FALSE stops R from adding an extra numbering column.

```{r}
write.csv(grades, "students_grades_processed.csv", row.names = FALSE)
```

Export the at-risk students.** The file is written only when there is at least one at-risk student.
```{r}
at_risk_df <- grades[!is.na(grades$AttendanceFlag) & grades$AttendanceFlag == "At Risk", ]

if (nrow(at_risk_df) > 0) {
  write.csv(at_risk_df, "at_risk_students.csv", row.names = FALSE)
  print("at_risk_students.csv exported successfully.")
} else {
  print("No at-risk students found; at_risk_students.csv was not written.")
}
```

Export the honors list.

Create a data frame honors with only the rows where Honors is "Yes".
Keep only these columns: StudentID, Name, Section, FinalGrade, Attendance. Hint: grades[rows_condition, c("StudentID", "Name")].
Use an if ... else statement to export it as honors_list.csv, or print a message if the list is empty.

```{r}
honors_rows <- !is.na(grades$Honors) & grades$Honors == "Yes"
honors <- grades[honors_rows, c("StudentID", "Name", "Section", "FinalGrade", "Attendance")]

if (nrow(honors) > 0) {
  write.csv(honors, "honors_list.csv", row.names = FALSE)
  print("honors_list.csv exported successfully.")
} else {
  print("Honors list is empty; honors_list.csv was not written.")
}
```

Verify your exports. Never assume a file was written correctly. Read it back and compare.

```{r}
# 1. Read back and compare the full processed table
grades_reloaded <- read.csv("students_grades_processed.csv", stringsAsFactors = FALSE)

cat("Processed row match:", identical(nrow(grades_reloaded), nrow(grades)), "\n")
cat("Processed col match:", identical(ncol(grades_reloaded), ncol(grades)), "\n")
cat("Processed names match:", identical(names(grades_reloaded), names(grades)), "\n")
print(head(grades_reloaded))

# 2. Read back and compare at-risk students (if exported)
if (file.exists("at_risk_students.csv")) {
  at_risk_reloaded <- read.csv("at_risk_students.csv", stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
  cat("At-risk row match:", identical(nrow(at_risk_reloaded), nrow(at_risk_df)), "\n")
  cat("At-risk col match:", identical(ncol(at_risk_reloaded), ncol(at_risk_df)), "\n")
  print(at_risk_reloaded)
} else {
  print("at_risk_students.csv does not exist (no at-risk students).")
}

# 3. Read back and compare the honors list (if exported)
if (file.exists("honors_list.csv")) {
  honors_reloaded <- read.csv("honors_list.csv", stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
  cat("Honors row match:", identical(nrow(honors_reloaded), nrow(honors)), "\n")
  cat("Honors col match:", identical(ncol(honors_reloaded), ncol(honors)), "\n")
  cat("Honors names match:", identical(names(honors_reloaded), names(honors)), "\n")
  print(honors_reloaded)
} else {
  print("honors_list.csv does not exist (honors list was empty).")
}
```

Question #8

How does the missing midterm appear in the exported file?
What would the file look like without row.names = FALSE? Try it with a temporary file name and compare.
```{r}
# 1. Export with row.names = FALSE (clean export)
write.csv(grades, "temp_no_rownames.csv", row.names = FALSE)

# 2. Export WITHOUT row.names = FALSE (defaults to row.names = TRUE)
write.csv(grades, "temp_with_rownames.csv")

# 3. Inspect raw lines directly from the text files
cat("--- Raw lines WITH row.names (default) ---\n")
writeLines(readLines("temp_with_rownames.csv", n = 7))

cat("\n--- Raw lines WITHOUT row.names (row.names = FALSE) ---\n")

# 4. Read both back into R and compare structure
df_with_rn <- read.csv("temp_with_rownames.csv", stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
df_no_rn   <- read.csv("temp_no_rownames.csv", stringsAsFactors = FALSE)

cat("\nColumns WITH row.names:", ncol(df_with_rn), "\n")
print(names(df_with_rn))

cat("\nColumns WITHOUT row.names:", ncol(df_no_rn), "\n")
print(names(df_no_rn))

# Find the row where Midterm was missing and see how it looks reloaded
missing_row <- which(is.na(grades$Midterm))
cat("\nRow(s) with missing Midterm:", missing_row, "\n")
print(df_no_rn[missing_row, c("StudentID", "Name", "Quiz", "Midterm", "Final", "FinalGrade", "Result", "Remarks")])

# 5. Clean up temporary files
unlink(c("temp_with_rownames.csv", "temp_no_rownames.csv"))
```

Question #9

a. Add a column Scholarship to grades using these rules, then export the qualified students.

```{r}
grades$Scholarship <- ifelse(
  is.na(grades$FinalGrade),
  "Pending",
  ifelse(
    !is.na(grades$Attendance) & grades$FinalGrade >= 95 & grades$Attendance >= 90,
    "Full",
    ifelse(
      !is.na(grades$Attendance) & grades$FinalGrade >= 85 & grades$Attendance >= 90,
      "Partial",
      "None"
    )
  )
)

# Check category counts
table(grades$Scholarship, useNA = "ifany")

# Filter qualified students ("Full" or "Partial")
qualified_scholarships <- grades[
  !is.na(grades$Scholarship) & grades$Scholarship %in% c("Full", "Partial"),
]

# Export if at least one qualified student exists
if (nrow(qualified_scholarships) > 0) {
  write.csv(qualified_scholarships, "scholarship_candidates.csv", row.names = FALSE)
  print("scholarship_candidates.csv exported successfully.")
  print(qualified_scholarships[, c("StudentID", "Name", "Section", "FinalGrade", "Attendance", "Scholarship")])
} else {
  print("No qualified scholarship candidates found; scholarship_candidates.csv was not written.")
}
```

Question #10

Answer in one or two sentences each, as comments.

Why did you check is.na() before comparing the final grade to a number?
ans.Comparing an `NA` value to a number in R returns `NA` rather than `FALSE`, which causes vectorized `ifelse()` to propagate `NA` instead of assigning `"Pending"`. Checking `is.na()` first isolates missing grades so numeric comparisons only run on actual numbers.

2. in Task 3.2, what would happen if the Failed condition were placed before the Incomplete condition?
ans.Checking **Failed** before **Incomplete** in R causes comparisons against a missing grade (`NA`) to evaluate to `NA` rather than labeling the student `"Incomplete"` first—propagating `NA` in vectorized `ifelse()` or throwing a missing-value error in a scalar `if ()` statement.

3. When is ifelse() the better choice than if ... else, and when is if ... else better?
ans. Use `ifelse()` for vectorized element-by-element transformations across columns or vectors, and use `if ... else` for scalar control flow, side effects, or branching execution blocks.

4. Why is it useful to read an exported CSV back into R?
ans.Reading an exported CSV back into R verifies that row counts, column names, missing values (`NA`), and formatting (such as avoiding extra row-name columns) were saved accurately rather than just assumed.
